sources.service_family: Google Cloud Run services and worker pools
sources.reviewer_note: Request-based adapters use the documented 0.167-vCPU/256-MiB function shape; worker pools use 1 vCPU/512 MiB and are billed for their full lifetime after the shared free tier.
Three internal and one external step are billed in separate 1,000-step increments.
Regional Standard-cluster management fee; the zonal free-tier credit is intentionally not applied.
On-demand e2-standard-8 node price in europe-west1; the scenario-specific node count is an allocation, not a provider price fact.
Balanced Persistent Disk capacity price; 100 GiB per node is a scenario allocation, not a provider price fact.
One external passthrough network load-balancer forwarding rule is modeled for the command boundary.
The fixed 30-day retention is included in log-bucket ingestion.
Existing reviewed premium-tier Europe internet-egress schedule is reused.
GCP has no managed MQTT replacement; the hosted broker must remain explicit.

sources.service_family: Google Cloud standalone MQTT broker architecture
sources.reviewer_note: Google's reference architecture routes incoming telemetry and outgoing commands through a standalone MQTT broker and connects backend workloads through Pub/Sub or another integration.
The previously selected 5.8.8 image is EOL at the research cut-off and is rejected.
A clustered supported EMQX deployment cannot produce a reproducible public software-price input.
Apache-2.0 avoids software-license cost, but ASF incubation remains an explicit PoC-only operational-maturity risk; Pub/Sub stays the durable command owner.
Provider and service-account bindings must constrain mapped workload attributes.

sources.service_family: AWS STS GetWebIdentityToken outbound identity federation
sources.reviewer_note: AWS uses STS GetWebIdentityToken for Azure's generic OIDC exchange. Outbound federation must be enabled for the account, the global STS endpoint is forbidden, and exact principal/audience claims remain deployment-bound.
The selected bridge deliberately configures ten records, partial batch responses, and five retries even though higher provider maxima exist.

sources.service_family: AWS Lambda SQS FIFO event-source mapping
sources.reviewer_note: A bridge-owned SQS FIFO subscription is the control-channel trigger; the Lambda is not invoked by a remote public endpoint.
Ordered telemetry landing uses serial PutRecord calls per device key; PutRecords is deliberately excluded because partial failure can reorder records.
Control landing maps device_id to MessageGroupId and event_id to MessageDeduplicationId; consumer idempotency remains mandatory beyond the broker window.
The selected bridge sets maxEventBatchSize to ten and only lets the trigger checkpoint after destination acceptance.
Control forwarding uses a session-enabled batched trigger, AutoCompleteMessages=false, and completes only accepted destination messages.

sources.service_family: Azure Event Hubs Microsoft Entra authorization
sources.reviewer_note: The destination role is scoped to the exact landing Event Hub; shared access keys and connection strings are disabled.
The bridge uses device_id as the partition key and never mixes device keys in a destination batch.

sources.service_family: Azure Service Bus Microsoft Entra authorization
sources.reviewer_note: The destination role is scoped to the exact control topic or queue and no SAS connection string is emitted.
Control landing maps device_id to SessionId and preserves order only within that session.
Small/Medium and Large control paths return success only after destination durable acceptance; a non-success response causes redelivery.
Large telemetry workers hold StreamingPull connections and acknowledge each source message only after destination acceptance.
Large telemetry uses manually dimensioned worker pools; unlike a Cloud Run service, the worker has no load-balanced endpoint.
Destination publishing enables ordering, uses europe-west1 endpoints, and keeps one active publisher sequence per device key.
External bridges authenticate through Workload Identity Federation and receive only topic-scoped publisher authorization.
The AWS-to-GCP path gives GCP Workload Identity Federation a signed GetCallerIdentity request whose response identifies the temporary AWS role.
The direct Pub/Sub pattern is for tens to hundreds of gateways and is not selected for the 100,000-device Large boundary.

sources.reviewer_note: The selected bundle therefore includes an explicit MQTT-to-Pub/Sub integration adapter; it is not hidden broker functionality.

sources.reviewer_note: Ordered shared subscriptions preserve the required per-device publication order while distributing load across adapter clients.
The Large allocation matches the published aggregate CPU and memory with 12 e2-standard-8 broker nodes, but the payload and software version differ; live 64-KiB testing remains mandatory.
Managed EMQX remains a valid functional alternative, but not a reproducibly priced Large optimizer input.
